profiles.meeting_scenario: An ML research lab is holding a 10-turn brainstorming meeting to shape an invited update survey article tentatively titled "Deep Neural Networks in Speech and Vision Systems: From Model Families to Real-World Deployment." The context is that an earlier broad survey in the area is now dated, and the team wants a sharper 2025 angle that still spans architectures, applications, and hardware constraints. The agenda is to generate and screen possible organizing frames for the paper, especially how to handle the "systems" angle, which application domains to include, and what kind of evidence to use in the efficiency section. The expected outcome is a provisional paper concept with a section structure and a shortlist of material to collect for the first outline.

members.name: Dr. Maya Chen
members.expertise: Multimodal deep learning, efficient inference, embedded AI systems
members.background: Leads a university lab on speech-vision models for robotics and mobile devices; previously worked on neural compression and edge deployment at an industrial research lab.
members.private_state: Wants the invited survey to be finished quickly, look authoritative for an upcoming edge-AI grant proposal, and remain clearly a survey rather than turning into a new experimental project that would expand scope and delay submission.
hidden_assumptions: When researchers say a paper has a strong "systems perspective," they usually mean the compute substrate around training and inference—memory, latency, power, accelerators, and deployment on constrained hardware.
A survey should synthesize reported results rather than generate new benchmark measurements, except perhaps for illustrative figures that do not become a core contribution.

In a speech-and-vision survey, "applications" mainly refers to tasks where the neural model directly consumes audio, images, or video, not larger decision-support workflows built on top of those features.
For this readership, cloud orchestration, data pipelines, and product-serving infrastructure are background context rather than central survey content.

members.name: Leo Martinez
members.expertise: Speech representation learning, reproducibility studies, ML systems reading and benchmarking
members.background: Finishing a dissertation on efficient speech encoders and has experience reproducing cross-paper latency and memory claims on shared lab hardware; often synthesizes literature across academic and industrial sources.
members.private_state: Wants the survey to be more than a conventional literature summary, ideally becoming a highly citable reference by tying model trends to operational practice and including some hands-on normalization of efficiency claims.
hidden_assumptions: In current ML discourse, a "systems" treatment naturally includes the full deployment stack: data collection loops, serving, cloud-edge partitioning, and production constraints, not just device-level inference.

If a survey claims to compare efficiency across papers, it is implicitly stronger to rerun a small subset on common hardware, because published latency numbers are too heterogeneous to stand on their own.

The phrase "applications of speech and vision" comfortably includes downstream domains such as precision medicine and transportation analytics even when speech or vision models are only one component in a larger pipeline.
Industrial case studies are most useful when they describe how organizations actually wire models into end-to-end products, not only what architecture appears in a public benchmark.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both agree the survey should have a strong "systems" section or "systems perspective."
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means hardware-aware model design and deployment constraints such as quantization, memory footprint, accelerator support, latency, and power on mobile, robots, and vehicles.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means the broader production stack around speech and vision models, including cloud-edge partitioning, serving architecture, data pipelines, and industrial deployment workflows.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The phrase sounds standard and high-level in ML meetings, and both members genuinely endorse it; each hears their preferred meaning as the obvious default, so no one feels a need to define it explicitly.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both say the survey should cover emerging "applications across disciplines" such as transportation and precision medicine.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 assumes this means applications where speech or vision models are themselves the main technical object—for example driver monitoring, visual inspection, keyword spotting, or onboard perception under hardware limits.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 assumes this includes larger interdisciplinary pipelines where speech or vision embeddings feed downstream models or decision systems, such as radiology triage workflows or fleet-risk monitoring platforms.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Because both mention the same domain labels and both value breadth, the difference in where the chapter boundary sits feels too natural and too secondary to trigger clarification during brainstorming.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both agree to create a table that "normalizes" latency, memory, and accuracy trade-offs across representative papers.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means harmonizing numbers already reported in the literature into common units and footnotes—for example converting batch sizes, latency units, and parameter counts into a consistent presentation.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means supplementing the table with a small in-house rerun of selected open-source checkpoints on a common testbed such as Jetson Orin and Pixel hardware so the numbers become directly comparable.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The word "normalize" plausibly covers either editorial harmonization or empirical remeasurement; in a survey-planning discussion, both options sound like sensible implementation details rather than a major methodological fork.

turns.inner_thought: The old survey was too broad and now it's dated. For this invited piece, I want a crisp 2025 update that looks authoritative for the grant and does not balloon into a new empirical project. The angle should be deployable speech-vision models: how model families changed under real hardware constraints, what compression and quantization trends matter, and how latency, memory, power, and accelerator compatibility shape choices on edge devices. If we frame it around systems, readers in embedded AI will immediately see the value.
